prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a rare case where one clean idea, trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels on the clock transition, was turned into a measurement that is better than anything before it. Katori proposed and first demonstrated the scheme and Ye's group took it to the 10^-18 regime with many-body clock physics. Clocks in several national laboratories now agree far below the caesium standard, so the result is reproduced, not a single measurement. It is built on atomic structure, where theory and experiment meet in the quantitative way I trust, and it opens relativistic geodesy, tests of constants and dark-matter searches. The two names are natural and the maturity is beyond doubt. I also think the committee would be well served by a prize this solid, whose interpretation will not be revised.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology can be read as a technical achievement rather than a discovery of something unexpected, and I care about that distinction myself. The field also sits close to earlier recognition: Hall and Hänsch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control). Ion-clock groups, and Lemonde, Takamoto and others in the early lattice demonstrations, have claims that a two-name prize does not cover. If the redefinition of the second is delayed, the practical argument for timing weakens. Against that, my main alternative, twisted bilayer graphene, is exciting but young and the pairing mechanism is not understood, so I hesitate to put it ahead of a result that is settled.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked the lattice clock seventh and asked whether it would be seen as technology and metrology rather than a physics discovery, and also noted the overlap with ion-clock credit such as Wineland.
responses.response: I take the worry seriously, because I separated technological prizes from discovery prizes in public myself. But a clock at 10^-18 is also a probe of nature: it tests whether constants drift, it measures gravitational redshift over a centimetre, and it constrains ultralight dark matter. The magic-wavelength idea is a genuine physics insight, not engineering. On Wineland, the ion-clock prize recognised control of single quantum systems; it did not recognise the many-atom lattice scheme that removes Doppler and recoil shifts while averaging over thousands of atoms. I think the two are distinct, though I accept the citation should be phrased around the lattice scheme and not around clocks in general.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the clock first for the same reasons I did, that precision limits knowledge and Katori and Ye form a clean pair, and he noted that the 2005 comb prize leaves room for the clock itself.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on the maturity. Where I want to be more careful than Kroll is the claim that other contributors are secondary. Lemonde and the SYRTE group, and the PTB and NIST groups, did important early and comparison work, and Ye's group also depends on the comb technology already recognised. I would keep the citation tied to the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its demonstration at record accuracy, so that the priority question does not need to be resolved. I also see Kroll's squeezed-light ranking as more crowded in attribution than the clock, which is a reason to prefer the clock.

responses.point: Johansson put circuit QED first, arguing it is a regime-opening step that follows the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits without duplicating it, and noted Girvin or Blais as a third name.
responses.response: Circuit QED is mature and important, and I do not dismiss it. My disagreement is about timing and credit. Kroll himself noted that the 2025 prize makes a return to superconducting circuits sensitive, and I share that worry: two prizes in successive years on the same platform would look like one subject rewarded twice. The credit is also harder, with four credited names and a real theory-experiment split that cannot be drawn cleanly at three. The clock has a cleaner two-name story. I would still keep B016 under discussion for a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators first and magic-angle graphene second, arguing the quantum spin Hall effect is a new class of matter that has been confirmed for fifteen years and is timely, possibly overdue.
responses.response: I agree that B036 is mature and the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp trio is coherent. I placed it fifth because Eriksson and others, and also Mehlig, point to the overlap with the 2016 prize and to the unresolved credit for Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D work. Condensed-matter priority disputes are where I am least secure and I will defer to Eriksson and Mehlig on how serious they are. If the committee finds the overlap tolerable, I could see B036 as a strong second choice, but I do not think it is clearly ahead of the clock on credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Ye's other clock work, including the Th-229 nuclear clock, should enter the citation, or whether it should be confined to the lattice clock.
Whether the experimental priority of Katori's group against the early Sr work of other groups is fully settled in the record.
How the committee will weigh a young but strikingly new field (twisted bilayer graphene) against a mature but incremental-looking metrology result.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of the credited names for B025 (Katori, Ye) appears among my listed collaborators, and I see no specific conflict. I work in atomic structure theory, which is adjacent to the clock field, and I should flag that closeness of field. I also have no connection to B022 or B037 that I know of, though the atom-optics community around B037 overlaps with mine.
